Un manuscrit decouvert en Espagne eclaire les origines de la projection de Mercator

January 2026 Courrier International Mercator, cartography, manuscript, Spain, El Escorial, astronomy, celestial globe, Renaissance, history of science, star tables
Read the source article

Quick summary

A professor from the University of Hasselt has discovered a lost Mercator manuscript hidden for over 450 years in Spain's El Escorial library, revealing the scientific foundations behind the famous cartographer's celestial globe and revolutionary mapping methods.

Key takeaways

  • Professor Koenraad Van Cleempoel discovered the manuscript by chance while researching at the Royal Site of El Escorial near Madrid
  • The four-volume manuscript, dating from around 1550, is the most complete document ever found in Mercator's own handwriting
  • The document contains approximately 50 pages of astronomical observations, new mathematical methods, astronomical instrument designs, and three remarkable star tables
  • One star table provides precise coordinates for 130 stars and forms the scientific basis for Mercator's 1551 celestial globe
  • The manuscript remained unnoticed for over 450 years in the library of El Escorial, built between 1562-1584 for Philip II of Spain
